answer:
Across a continuous, multi-day round-the-clock TVAC campaign with minimal schedule margin, the greatest exposure is less the test environment itself than the human and procedural seams around it: crew handover, facility protection logic, GSE handling, and the temptation to trim verification against a fixed launch date.

### 1. Protection-circuit override during an off-nominal reading
A chamber operator can distrust a correctly-functioning alarm/fail-safe and continue the run, exposing hardware beyond qualification limits. In 1993, Mars Observer's flight Payload Data System was driven to -47°C (limit -20°C) when the chamber operator overrode alarm and fail-safe circuits, trusting a recently calibrated controller instead; a subsystem engineer on a separate data feed caught it and called for termination ([LLIS 274: Mars Observer Payload Data System (PDS) Exposure to Low Temperature](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/274)). Investigators recommended requiring hardware-engineering sign-off before any override of fail-safe devices, and continuous QA monitoring of environmental tests.

Check: confirm the abort procedure explicitly forbids a console operator from overriding a redline/fail-safe alone, and that cognizant subsystem engineers have an independent data feed and veto during every shift, not just day shift.

### 2. Lifting/installation GSE instability going into the chamber
Moving a flight vehicle with shrouding into a TVAC chamber on custom fixturing is itself a hazardous operation. TOPEX/POSEIDON's T/V fixture assembly rotated ~135° while being craned into the chamber in 1992 because the lifted configuration had never been stability-analyzed and the GSE design review had been repeatedly postponed ([LLIS 1089: TOPEX/POSEIDON Spacecraft Handling Anomaly Special Review Board Final Report](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1089)). Recommendations: no lifting equipment used without a full stability analysis of the complete loaded configuration, GSE drawings/analysis available 60 days before test, and a true precursor dry run with a representative mass mockup.

Check: verify the chamber-install lift fixture has a documented stability analysis for this spacecraft's as-built mass properties and that a full-fidelity dry run was actually performed, not substituted by a partial one.

### 3. Contamination of cold, sensitive optics/sensors
Standard outgassing material criteria can still allow contamination that cripples cold detectors. WF/PC-1's CCDs lost sensitivity during thermal-vacuum testing from contamination traced to the instrument itself, exposing that conventional ASTM E595 criteria are inadequate for instruments cold enough to trap films ([LLIS 352: Contamination Control for Susceptible Instruments](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/352)). Recommended: define instrument-specific sensitivity objectives and matching design/decontamination criteria rather than relying on generic material screening.

Check: confirm the payload has explicit, instrument-level contamination allowables for its coldest operating points, not just generic outgassing specs for the whole vehicle.

### 4. Schedule pressure truncating the verification program
Fixed-window schedules can quietly cut test content. SEASAT's antenna shipped without full gain/pattern measurement due to schedule pressure, and the subsequent system test failed its primary objective with no pre-test baseline to diagnose why ([LLIS 365: Antenna Performance Specifications Not Met](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/365)). Recommendation: any reduction or deletion of test content must be documented with its risk and explicitly accepted by the project, not just the test team.

Check: any TVAC content trimmed to protect shipment date should be logged with a stated performance-verification gap and signed off above the test team.

This is a research aid drawn from historical NASA records, not a substitute for a formal safety review.
